header: (Qaisar and another versus The State and another)
Appellants with Mr. James Joseph & Ch. Abdul Hafeez, advocates.
State by Mr. Waheed Rafique, DDPP.
Complainant by Mehar Habib Ullah Garwah and Mehar Yasir Habib,
body: GHULAM SARWAR NIHUNG, J:- Through this criminal appeal filed under Section 410 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 (Cr.P.C.), the appellants Qaisar and Shamsher Ahmad have assailed the judgment dated 06.07.2019 passed by the learned Additional Sessions Judge, Karor Lal Eason, District Layyah in case FIR No. 245/2016, dated 20.06.2016, registered under sections 302, 337-F(v), 148, 149, 109 PPC at Police Station Fatehpur, District Layyah, whereby he convicted and sentenced the appellants as under:- Under Section 302(b) PPC Life imprisonment as Ta’zir each for committing Qatl-e- Amd of Muhammad Aslam deceased with compensation of Rs. 5,00,000/- each payable to the legal heirs of the deceased under section 544-A Cr.P.C., in default thereof to undergo imprisonment for six months each. Benefit of Section 382-B Cr.P.C. was also extended to the appellants.

2. The convict-appellants, namely, Qaisar and Shamsher Ahmad have called in question the impugned judgment through Crl. A.No.847 of 2019 whereas Mehr Ali, complainant has filed Crl. Revision No.303 of 2019 for enhancement of sentence awarded to the appellants. Both these interconnected cases are being disposed of together through this single judgment. Crl. Appeal No.847 of 2019 (2)

3. Briefly, the prosecution case as set out in para-2 of trial court judgment is as under:- “Brief facts of this private complaint Ex.PP, are that Mehar Ali complainant is resident of Chak No.238/TDA and is an agriculturist. That on 20.06.2016 at about 02:30/03:00 P.M, the complainant along with Muhammad Aslam (brother) and Muhammad Latif s/o Ghulam Muhammad (nephew)

purchased some household articles from Qasba Fatehpur. During this Muhammad Riaz s/o Dost Muhammad, Caste Bhango, R/o Chak No.238/TDA also met them. After purchasing household articles, Muhammad Latif (nephew) and Muhammad Aslam (brother) proceeded to their house on motorcycle. That after some time, the complainant along with Muhammad Riaz also proceeded to their house on a motor car. When they reached on a link road Chak No.239-B/TDA, Muhammad Aslam and Muhammad Latif were going in front of them at some distance. In the meanwhile, accused Qaiser s/o Muhammad Sadiq, Muhammad Munir s/o Muhammad Mushtaq, Sarfaraz Ahmed s/o Faiz Ahmed, Shamsher Ahmed s/o Haji Zafar, Ashfaq Ahmed s/o Ishaq all armed with 30- Bore pistols, except Sarfaraz who was armed with repeater, Muhammad Javed s/o Mushtaq, Muhammad Naseer s/o Mushtaq, Sadiq s/o Mirza Khan, Muhammad Shehzad s/o Boota, Haji Zafar s/o Nawab Khan, Muhammad Irshad s/o Muhammad Yousaf and Muhammad Aslam s/o Ghulam Rasool, all armed with 'Sotas' on cars Suzuki Mehran and 2.OD white colour as well as on motorcycles while crossing the complainant emerged there. All the accused persons intercepted Muhammad Latif PW and Muhammad Aslam (brother) and they also encircled them. Qaiser accused while brandishing his pistol raised a lalkara while saying that you have to see that how many Ch. Sarwar, have came there. That after this all the accused persons de-boarded themselves from their respective vehicles. Qaiser accused made a fire with pistol on Muhammad Aslam which landed on his right leg and he fell down. Muhammad Shehzad made a blow of sota which landed on the right wrist. Shamsher accused made a second fire which landed on his left leg and he simmered. Who smeared with blood. Then Muhammad Munir, Ashfaq and Sarfaraz made fires with their respective weapons which landed on both the legs of Muhammad Aslam deceased. Muhammad Aslam accused (since died) took out scissor and cut right mustache. The accused persons threatened them if, someone came near, he will also be done to death. That due to fear, we did not came near. Muhammad Aslam accused (since died) made a blow of sota on the right scapula while Muhammad Javed accused made a sota blow on left scapula. Sarfaraz accused put Muhammad Aslam deceased while facing downward then Sadiq, Haji Zafar, Muhammad Naseer, Muhammad Irshad and Muhammad Javed, accused persons made sota blows on his thighs, waist and buttocks, who Crl. Appeal No.847 of 2019 (3)

became unconscious. That on hue and cry, the peoples of surroundings and passer by gathered there. The accused persons while seeing the peoples fled away from the spot on their vehicles along with their respective weapons. The complainant along with PWs rescued Muhammad Aslam (brother of complainant), who was in fasting condition. The complainant and PWs shifted him to hospital in the car but he succumbed to the injuries.

Motive behind the occurrence was that Muhammad Aslam deceased was head of complainant's family and there was a dispute of Ahata with Muhammad Aslam accused (since died). That in a melee the respondent party became injured and a case FIR No.63/15 was got registered against the deceased Muhammad Aslam and the complainant. That during investigation Muhammad Aslam deceased was found not involved while, the complainant along with others were convicted vide judgment dated 10.06.2016. That due to this grudge of Ahata, the all the accused persons hatched the conspiracy under the command of Kaleem Ullah Police constable and committed the brutal murder of Muhammad Aslam deceased”.

On the statement of complainant Mehar Ali, Ex.PA, case FIR No.245/16, Dated 20.06.2016 Exh.PA/1, under sections 302/337F(v)/148/149/109 of PPC, was got registered at Police Sstation, Fatehpur against the accused persons. That police did not conduct the investigation on merit. Feeling aggrieved by the investigation of police, the complainant filed private complaint Exh.PP wherein cursory evidence was recorded and the accused were summoned to face trial. Charge was framed against them on 19.01.2018 to which they pleaded not guilty and claimed trial. In order to prove its case, the prosecution examined as many as thirteen witnesses whereas Muhammad Afzal SI was produced as CW-1 and after tendering documentary evidence the prosecution closed the evidence. In their statements recorded under Section 342 Cr.P.C., the appellants refuted the allegations and professed their innocence. However, they neither opted to appear as their own witnesses on oath under section 340(2) Cr.P.C. nor adduced any evidence in their defence. After the conclusion of the trial, the learned trial court convicted and sentenced the appellants as detailed above, hence the instant appeal.
Crl. Appeal No.847 of 2019 (4)
5. Arguments heard. Record perused.

6. The occurrence took place on 20.06.2016 at 2:30/3:00 p.m., the fard bayyan was recorded from the mouth of the Mehr Ali complainant PW-11 at THQ Hospital at 4:00 p.m. and the FIR was lodged at 4/5 p.m. after an unexplained delay of 2 to 2½ hours. Although such a delay may not appear inordinate on the face of it yet the manner in which the prosecution attempted to explain it renders the delay fatal. The complainant asserted that the police were immediately alerted via the emergency helpline "15", whereupon police officials arrived at the hospital. However, neither any record of the purported "15" call was produced in evidence nor was any police official examined to substantiate that such prior information was ever received. Had the police been promptly notified on "15", there would have been no plausible reason for delaying the formal recording of the FIR under Section 154 Cr.P.C. until 4:00/5:00 p.m. The requirement of prompt registration of information under Section 154 Cr.P.C. is designed to obtain an early and untainted account of the occurrence before there is time for fabrication. In a case hinging primarily on ocular account, this unexplained and uncorroborated delay leaves ample room for consultation, deliberation, and embellishment. Reliance in this regard is placed upon Zeeshan alias Shani v. The State (2012 SCMR 428) and “Manzar Abbas and another v. The State”(2025 SCMR 1024).

7. According to complainant Mehr Ali (PW-11), on 20.06.2016, he, along with his brother Muhammad Aslam (deceased) and nephew Muhammad Latif (PW-12), went to Fatehpur to purchase household articles and was returning home when the incident occurred. During cross-examination, PW-11 admitted that he did not show the purchased household articles to the Investigating Officer (I.O.) at the spot, claiming instead that the items were lying in the diggi of a motorcar. Had Crl. Appeal No.847 of 2019 (5)

those articles been produced before the I.O., they would have served as tangible proof of the witnesses' presence at the scene. Their non-production remains wholly unexplained. PW-11 further conceded in cross-examination that previous enmity existed between the parties and admitted that although Muhammad Latif (PW-12) and the deceased were riding the same motorcycle, neither PW-12 nor any part of the motorcycle sustained a single firearm hit. It is highly improbable that a large, heavily armed group of assailants, actuated by admitted enmity, would single out only the deceased while leaving the accompanying eye-witnesses and their motorcycle entirely unscathed. Such unnatural conduct necessitates that the presence of the eye-witnesses be established through cogent and independent corroboration, which is conspicuously absent in the instant case.

Further, the complainant deposed that he transported the injured Muhammad Aslam to the hospital in a motorcar. However, he admitted during cross-examination that he never produced the said vehicle before the I.O. on the pretext that the I.O. did not demand its custody. The motorcar, being a vital piece of circumstantial evidence to establish the shifting of the injured, the complainant’s presence at the spot and the time of arrival at the hospital was withheld. No explanation was offered as to why the I.O. failed to take the vehicle into possession nor was the driver of the car produced as a witness. This glaring omission casts serious doubt upon the prosecution’s narrative regarding the shifting of the deceased to the hospital. Furthermore, PW-11 admitted in cross-examination that his clothes became stained with the blood of his injured brother, yet he failed to hand them over to the I.O. on the same excuse that the officer did not ask for them. A witness who claims to have lifted and shifted a profusely bleeding victim would inevitably have blood-stained garments. The failure to produce those Crl. Appeal No.847 of 2019 (6)

clothes which constituted the best corroborative evidence of his presence and participation under Article 71 of the Qanun-e- Shahadat Order, 1984 cannot be brushed aside as a mere investigative lapse rather it strikes at the very root of his claimed presence at the crime scene. Taken together, the nonproduction of these material articles attracts an adverse presumption against the prosecution under Article 129(g) of the Qanun-e-Shahadat Order, 1984, that had such evidence been produced, it would not have supported the prosecution version. As regards Muhammad Latif (PW-12), he candidly stated in his examination-in-chief that out of fear, he fled across the road and concealed himself inside a citrus orchard. A witness who ran away and hid to save his life could not reasonably be expected to observe the incident in the minute detail narrated by him. Notably, the learned trial court itself refrained from placing implicit reliance upon the testimony of PW-12. Reliance is placed upon “Munir Ahmad and 3 others v. The State and others” (2026 SCMR 1498) and Shahzad Tanveer v. The State (2012 SCMR 172).

8. The inquest report (Exh. PF) was prepared by the I.O. wherein Ghulam Muhammad (PW-1) and Niaz Ahmed were recorded as the persons who identified the dead body. Similarly, the post-mortem report reflects that the very same witnesses identified the corpse at the time of autopsy. Had the complainant shifted the injured to the hospital and remained present throughout, he would have been the most natural person to identify his deceased brother. His absence at these crucial stages militates heavily against his claimed presence at the occurrence. Reliance is placed upon “Mst. Sughra Begum and another v. Qaiser Pervez and others” (2015 SCMR 1142).

9. Dr. Muhammad Asim (PW-6), who conducted the autopsy, testified that the dead body was received at the hospital at 3:30 p.m., whereas the police papers were handed over to him at 8:00 p.m., following which he performed the Crl. Appeal No.847 of 2019 (7)

post-mortem examination. This reflects an inordinate delay of more than five hours in conducting the autopsy, for which no plausible explanation was tendered by the prosecution. This unexplained delay contravenes the mandatory provisions of Police Rules, 1934, which requires the prompt dispatch of the dead body along with complete police papers to the Medical Officer. Such a delay speaks volumes and lends credence to the inference that the intervening time was consumed in consultations and fabricating the prosecution story after the arrival of the dead body at the hospital. Reliance is placed upon “Irshad Ahmed v. The State” (2011 SCMR 1190) and “Muhammad alias Ahmad v. The State” (2025 SCMR 2052).

10. The prosecution placed heavy reliance on the recovery of two 30-bore pistols effected on 16.08.2016 at the pointation of the appellants alongside three crime empties secured from the spot on the day of occurrence which were dispatched to the Punjab Forensic Science Agency (PFSA), Lahore, on 23.08.2016. While the PFSA report (Exh. PDD) returned positive, confirming that the crime empties matched the recovered pistols. It is pertinent to note that while the strict rigours of Section 103 Cr.P.C. may not apply to every recovery on pointation, the complete omission to associate any independent witness from the locality, despite the recoveries being effected nearly two months after the incident, renders them highly doubtful. Even otherwise, it is a settled principle of criminal jurisprudence that recovery of a weapon is merely corroborative in nature. Where the direct ocular account has been disbelieved, a positive forensic report cannot, by itself, form the basis of a conviction. At best, the PFSA report establishes that the empties were fired from the recovered pistols, but in the absence of trustworthy direct evidence, it fails to connect the appellants with the firing of those shots. Reliance is placed upon “Muhammad Nasir Butt and 2 others v. The State and others” (2025 SCMR 662).
Crl. Appeal No.847 of 2019 (8)

11. The prosecution alleged a motive stemming from a dispute over Ahata and Lumberdari, coupled with a previous criminal case registered under section 324 PPC. However, it is an admitted position on record that in the said earlier case, the complainant party was convicted, whereas Muhammad Aslam (deceased) was declared innocent by the police. Viewed in this backdrop, the alleged motive was equally available to the complainant party to falsely implicate the appellants. Motive is universally recognized as a double-edged weapon, while it may prompt an accused to commit an offence, it can equally motivate a complainant to falsely rope in adversaries, particularly where enmity is admitted and parties are embroiled in property litigation. In the absence of credible ocular evidence, motive alone cannot bridge the evidentiary gaps in the prosecution case. Significantly, the learned trial court itself acquitted nine co-accused against whom the exact same motive was attributed, thereby demonstrating that the motive was not deemed sufficient to sustain a conviction. Reliance is placed upon “Muhammad Ashraf alias Acchu v. The State (2019 SCMR 652) and “Manzar Abbas and another v. The State” (2025 SCMR 1024).

12. The learned trial court, while acquitting co-accused Sarfraz Ahmad who as per prosecution case made a single fire with his repeater gun hitting on both legs of Muhammad Aslam deceased, Muhammad Munir who made fire with pistol which landed on the right leg of Muhammad Aslam deceased, Muhammad Javaid who made a sota blow on the left scapula of Muhammad Aslam deceased, Muhammad Nasir Hussain and Muhammad Irshad who were assigned general role of beating, Sadiq, Haji Zafar and Kaleem Ullah who were assigned the role of abetment and Muhammad Shahzad who made a sota blow landed on right wrist of Muhammad Aslam deceased, has disbelieved the very same eye-witnesses, the same recovery and the same medical evidence, on the ground that the prosecution Crl. Appeal No.847 of 2019 (9)

evidence was contradictory, discrepant and not worthy of reliance. It is an admitted position that the evidence against the appellant is not separate, independent or distinct from the evidence produced against the acquitted co-accused. Furthermore, the complainant Mehr Ali filed Crl. Appeal No.925 of 2019 titled “Mehr Ali versus The State,e tc.” against the acquittal of the co-accused persons which was dismissed as having been withdrawn on 09.02.2026 by a learned Division Bench of this Court. Therefore, their acquittal has attained finality and the findings recorded by the learned trial court disbelieving the prosecution witnesses have become conclusive against the prosecution. It is settled law that where co-accused are acquitted on the same set of evidence, the conviction of the appellant on that very evidence cannot be sustained. The prosecution cannot be permitted to approbate and reprobate. The acquittal of the co-accused on the same evidence, therefore, furnishes an additional and strong ground for extending the benefit of doubt to the appellant. Reliance in this regard may be placed upon “Maqsood Alam and another v. The State and others” (2024 SCMR 156) and “Muhammad Nawaz and another v. The State and others” (2024 SCMR 1731).

13. It is an axiomatic principle of criminal justice that to extend the benefit of doubt to an accused, it is not necessary that there be multiple circumstances creating suspicion rather, a single circumstance that creates a reasonable doubt in a prudent mind regarding the guilt of the accused entitles him to acquittal not as a matter of grace or concession but as a matter of right. Reliance in this regard may be placed upon “Laiq Shah v. The State” (2026 SCMR 257), “Muhammad Ehsan Shah v. The State through A.G., Islamabad and another” (2025 SCMR 730) and “Ali Imran and others v. The State and another” (2026 SCMR 1370).
14. For the reasons recorded hereinabove, this Court holds that the FIR was lodged after an unexplained delay; that the Crl. Appeal No.847 of 2019 (10)

presence of the complainant and eye-witnesses at the crime scene is shrouded in doubt; that the prosecution withheld the best available evidence by failing to produce the motorcar, household articles, and blood-stained clothes of the complainant; that the substantial delay in conducting the postmortem examination remained unexplained; that the recovery of weapons and positive PFSA report, being merely corroborative, cannot sustain a conviction once the ocular account is discarded and that the alleged motive, being a double-edged weapon, fails to strengthen the prosecution case. Resultantly, the prosecution has failed to prove its case against the appellants beyond a shadow of reasonable doubt.

15. Consequently, Criminal Appeal No. 847 of 2019 is allowed. The conviction and sentences recorded against the appellants, Qaisar and Shamsher Ahmad, under Section 302(b) PPC by the learned Additional Sessions Judge, Karor Lal Eason, District Layyah, vide judgment dated 06.07.2019, are hereby set aside and they are acquitted of the charge by extending them the benefit of the doubt. Since the appellants are already on bail, their sureties are discharged.

16. In view of the acceptance of the appeal against conviction and the consequent acquittal of the appellants, Criminal Revision No. 303 of 2019, seeking enhancement of their sentence is accordingly dismissed.
(GHULAM SARWAR NIHUNG)
JUDGE Approved for reporting.
JUDGE Iftikhar
